frictionVectors.title: European energy diversification
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas but is expanding alternative suppliers and renewable capacity, gradually weakening Algeria's bargaining leverage. State control over hydrocarbons remains firm.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Western Sahara tensions
frictionVectors.details: Rivalry with Morocco and instability across the Sahel raise security costs and complicate regional energy and transport ambitions. External powers are competing for influence along Algeria's southern borders.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting U.S. and European backing as a route for critical minerals, increasing Angola's geopolitical leverage. Competition with Chinese infrastructure and financing interests remains intense.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil still dominates export earnings and fiscal stability, leaving Luanda exposed to price swings and declining production. International operators retain substantial influence over upstream technology and capital.

frictionVectors.title: Regional trade disruption
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger and shifting Sahel alliances threaten transit flows through the Port of Cotonou. Benin is balancing commercial interdependence with sovereignty and border-security concerns.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Militant infiltration from Burkina Faso and Niger is increasing demand for foreign training, intelligence, and equipment. Expanded security partnerships could constrain policy autonomy if conditions worsen.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong state leverage in its diamond partnership but remains exposed to synthetic diamonds, weaker global demand, and negotiations with major producers. Revenue concentration limits room for fiscal error.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, lithium, and other minerals is growing, creating opportunities for diversification. The government must preserve transparent licensing and domestic value capture as new investors arrive.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control struggle
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production and processing, but informal mining, smuggling, and opaque security-linked networks continue to drain value. Foreign buyers and intermediaries remain embedded in the trade.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Expanded reliance on Russian-linked security personnel offers the government an alternative to Western partners but risks opaque payment arrangements and resource-linked influence. Persistent jihadist violence limits effective state control over mining zones.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Governance
frictionVectors.details: Bujumbura is seeking greater state control and formalization of gold and nickel exports, but limited oversight and informal cross-border networks reduce public capture of mineral value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed groups and cross-border accusations, disrupting trade and constraining Burundi's regional economic options.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, and digital connectivity depend heavily on European, Chinese, and multilateral financing, creating long-term exposure to external creditors and operators.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Trafficking
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's Atlantic position makes it a transit point for narcotics and a target for illicit maritime networks, requiring sustained foreign security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Mining Capture
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon, mining, and infrastructure projects remain shaped by foreign firms and opaque domestic patronage, limiting broad-based sovereign returns.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict
frictionVectors.details: The armed conflict in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten roads, agricultural production, and extractive investment while increasing dependence on external security and humanitarian actors.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak state control allows foreign-linked companies, armed groups, and informal traders to capture substantial value from gold and diamonds, especially outside Bangui.

frictionVectors.title: Africa Corps Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian security personnel has strengthened regime protection but deepened strategic dependence and enabled opaque access to mining concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains heavily dependent on oil revenues managed through state-linked structures, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price shocks and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Spillover
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan is driving refugees, arms flows, and militia risks across the eastern border, increasing pressure on Chadian infrastructure and security resources.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros territorial dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration pressure and maritime enforcement keep the dispute politically active. The issue constrains bilateral relations and limits Comoros's control over surrounding waters.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on external infrastructure funding
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, and connectivity projects rely heavily on foreign donors and Gulf or Asian partners. Limited domestic fiscal capacity reduces Comoros's leverage over project terms and long-term strategic assets.

highlights: Eastern sovereignty is under persistent pressure

frictionVectors.title: Conflict around North and South Kivu
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, regional security competition, and illicit mineral networks continue to undermine Kinshasa's authority in the east. External military and political involvement complicates efforts to secure territory and formalize mining activity.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper supply-chain leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-linked buyers retain major influence over copper and cobalt extraction, processing, and transport. The government is seeking more local value addition, but infrastructure gaps and security risks limit sovereign bargaining power.

highlights: Debt and infrastructure ties limit autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy and public finances remain highly exposed to offshore oil production and foreign operating partners. Price volatility and limited domestic refining capacity weaken the state's ability to convert resource wealth into broad-based sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: External debt-linked infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and other foreign financing remain central to roads, ports, and public works. Debt obligations and project concentration can constrain policy flexibility and increase outside influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance in cocoa value chains
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened producer regulation and is pursuing greater domestic processing, but multinational traders and manufacturers still capture substantial downstream value. Price exposure and farmer incomes remain vulnerable to external market conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Northern border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist spillover from the Sahel continues to pressure border communities and security spending. International assistance supports surveillance and counterterrorism capacity, but reliance on partners creates a continuing sovereignty trade-off.

highlights: Ports remain the core strategic asset

frictionVectors.title: Competition among foreign military powers
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. This generates revenue and deterrence but exposes the country to great-power rivalry and limits independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Port revenues and logistics infrastructure are central to the economy, while debt exposure and contested concessions have increased sensitivity to external creditors and operators. Regional competition and instability around the Red Sea add further pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and foreign-exchange shortages keep Egypt reliant on IMF, Gulf, and other external financing, limiting policy autonomy over strategic assets and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains Cairo's central sovereignty and resource-security concern, with negotiations unable to produce a durable operating agreement.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing Oil and Gas Fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling hydrocarbon output is weakening state revenue while the government seeks foreign partners and new investment to sustain LNG and gas-processing infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque External Concessions
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and foreign contractors retain significant influence over production and infrastructure, while opaque contracts constrain public accountability and domestic value capture.

highlights: Mining Revenues Under Tight State Control

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb attract interest from Gulf and other external powers, increasing pressure over ports, access, and military relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but rely on foreign operators and remain exposed to sanctions, reputational risks, and concentrated commodity markets.

frictionVectors.title: External Trade Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's fiscal position and access to regional markets depend heavily on SACU transfers and South African transport, energy, and logistics networks.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and Industrial Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, soft-drink concentrates, and light manufacturing remain vulnerable to changing trade preferences, water constraints, and decisions by foreign-linked investors.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over domestic electricity generation but continues to generate acute friction with Egypt and Sudan over filling and long-term operations.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and multilateral financing remains important for transport, power, and telecommunications, while debt restructuring and internal conflict constrain sovereign bargaining power.

highlights: Oil and Manganese Remain Strategic Anchors

frictionVectors.title: French Economic Footprint
frictionVectors.details: France retains commercial and historical influence in energy, mining, and services, although Libreville is seeking more diversified partnerships and greater domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: The transition authorities are under pressure to convert oil and manganese wealth into local processing, jobs, and fiscal gains rather than relying on concession-based exports.

highlights: Port and Tourism Drive Economic Dependence

frictionVectors.title: Regional Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegalese territory and cooperation for overland trade, energy connectivity, and security, limiting its strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Banjul Port Capacity
frictionVectors.details: Port limitations and dependence on external logistics investment constrain the country's ability to capture more value from transit trade and agricultural exports.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain deeply embedded in gold production and marketing, while Ghana seeks greater domestic refining, formalization, and fiscal capture.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-Linked Illegal Mining Networks
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining involving foreign financiers and equipment damages water systems and farmland, challenging state authority and generating public pressure for tougher enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou External Consortiums
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed and international consortiums dominate the capital-intensive Simandou iron-ore project, creating a persistent tension between infrastructure delivery and Guinean control of future rents.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains reliant on foreign operators, railways, and export terminals for bauxite, with limited domestic processing and significant exposure to external commodity demand.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign buyers, volatile prices, and weak domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Transnational Criminal Influence
frictionVectors.details: Drug-trafficking networks exploit weak institutions and maritime access, undermining customs control, political accountability, and the state's ability to secure strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy obligations to international lenders and bilateral creditors constrain fiscal autonomy and limit Nairobi's room to renegotiate major infrastructure and development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional interests compete for influence across ports, logistics, energy, and digital infrastructure, creating concerns over long-term control of critical assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but make Lesotho highly dependent on Pretoria for infrastructure financing, market access, and operational security.

frictionVectors.title: Political and Fiscal Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Coalition instability and limited domestic revenue reduce the government's bargaining power with external financiers and South African institutions.

highlights: Port and Rail Access Attract Foreign Capital

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining concessions remain central to exports and public revenue, leaving Liberia exposed to commodity cycles and disputes over local benefits, land, and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Access Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors and lenders are positioned to influence rail, port, and logistics development, creating recurring tension between urgently needed infrastructure and long-term national control.

highlights: Oil Revenue Divided by Rival Authorities

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks compete over oil facilities, budget flows, and appointments, weakening the National Oil Corporation's effective national control.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Foreign Military Footprints
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian-linked, and other external actors retain influence through security partnerships and military infrastructure, limiting Libya's strategic autonomy and complicating reunification.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining operations provide export income but generate disputes over taxation, environmental damage, land rights, and the distribution of local benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Market Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and development partners remain central to transport, energy, and mining infrastructure, leaving Madagascar vulnerable to external pressure over concessions and policy stability.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt distress and reliance on IMF, World Bank, and bilateral creditors limit fiscal room and influence decisions on subsidies, agriculture, and public assets.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Minerals Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium, rare-earth, and niobium projects could diversify exports, but weak institutional capacity creates risks of unfavorable contracts and limited local value capture.

highlights: Junta asserts control over gold resources

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontations
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing foreign mining operators for higher state participation and tax compliance, increasing legal and diplomatic friction with international investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel provides regime support but reduces strategic autonomy and exposes mining corridors and infrastructure to opaque external influence.

highlights: Gas exports are reshaping national leverage

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Gas Project
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-linked offshore project offers new fiscal and geopolitical leverage, but foreign operators, project delays, and revenue-sharing arrangements limit near-term sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The mining-to-port rail system remains central to export earnings and is vulnerable to commodity-price swings, infrastructure bottlenecks, and dependence on foreign technical capital.

highlights: Indian Ocean diplomacy is strategically active
Economic sovereignty rests on services and ports

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Maritime Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos settlement process remains central to Mauritius's territorial claims and regional influence, while implementation details and external security interests continue to generate uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius must balance Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf commercial interests in ports, logistics, and digital infrastructure without compromising its non-aligned posture.

highlights: Western Sahara remains the sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, and renewable-energy projects in the territory generate investment and state revenue but remain exposed to legal challenges and opposition from the Polisario Front and Algeria.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding renewables, desalination, and green-hydrogen capacity, yet remains exposed to imported hydrocarbons, water scarcity, and foreign technology and capital.

highlights: LNG Ambitions Constrained by Cabo Delgado

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique's liquefied natural gas projects remain dominated by foreign operators, financing, and export infrastructure. Delays and security risks limit state leverage over the timing and distribution of revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten offshore gas logistics and onshore transport corridors. Rwanda's security role improves protection but adds reliance on an external military partner.

highlights: Oil and Green Hydrogen Raise Strategic Stakes

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries could strengthen Namibia's fiscal position, but development remains dependent on international oil companies, foreign technology, and export finance. Local-content and fiscal negotiations will shape how much value remains domestic.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects rely on European, Gulf, and other external capital and offtake agreements. The government is seeking industrial spillovers while managing concerns over land, water, and energy sovereignty.

highlights: Western Exit Opens Russian Security Channel

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating longstanding French-linked mining arrangements and seeking greater state control over uranium revenues. Production and export capacity remain vulnerable to political rupture, sanctions, and weak logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reduced Western military involvement has increased reliance on Russian security cooperation and regional partners. This may reinforce regime autonomy while adding new external leverage over strategic sites and transport corridors.

highlights: Oil Theft Still Erodes Sovereign Revenue

frictionVectors.title: Oil-Sector Infrastructure Gaps
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining expansion offers Nigeria greater control over fuel supply, but pipelines, terminals, and upstream production remain exposed to sabotage, theft, and foreign technical dependence. Declining output limits the immediate sovereignty gains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Divestment
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies are reshaping their Nigerian portfolios while new investors seek opportunities in deepwater and gas assets. Regulatory uncertainty and financing needs constrain Abuja's bargaining power over long-term resource development.

highlights: Minerals and Regional Security Drive Leverage

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and mineral-trading networks remain under intense international scrutiny over alleged links to conflict minerals and support for armed actors. Diplomatic pressure could affect trade access and external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Technology Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strong domestic state capacity coexists with reliance on foreign aid, concessional finance, and imported technology for infrastructure and services. Kigali is diversifying toward Gulf and Asian partners to reduce dependence on Western donors.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon exploration in the Gulf of Guinea offers potential revenue but leaves the country dependent on foreign capital and technical expertise. Commercial viability and transparent licensing remain unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND EEZ CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Limited naval and monitoring capacity constrains enforcement against illegal fishing and weakens São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining position with distant-water fleets.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN ENERGY OPERATORS
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas production provides Dakar with stronger fiscal and diplomatic leverage, but major projects remain reliant on foreign operators, lenders, and technology. Revenue governance and contract renegotiation are politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: GTA BORDER INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Mauritania requires sustained cross-border coordination over revenue, gas processing, security, and maritime jurisdiction.

frictionVectors.title: DISTANT-WATER FISHING
frictionVectors.details: Foreign tuna fleets generate essential economic activity but create persistent sovereignty concerns over licensing value, stock depletion, and enforcement inside Seychelles' extensive maritime zone.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Port, surveillance, and maritime-security cooperation with India, China, and Western partners offers capacity gains while exposing the islands to pressure to align with competing strategic blocs.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports and fiscal expectations, but foreign ownership, commodity-price exposure, and environmental costs limit domestic control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: FREETOWN PORT AND CORRIDORS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port and transport infrastructure can improve trade capacity, yet concession terms, debt exposure, and strategic access remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA AND INDIAN OCEAN ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Competing Turkish, Gulf, Ethiopian, and Western interests in ports and maritime access intersect with Somalia's claims over its territorial waters and federal authority. External partnerships provide infrastructure and security but can deepen internal political disputes.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE GOVERNANCE AND FEDERALISM
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, fisheries, and port revenues remain constrained by weak institutions, federal-government tensions, and al-Shabaab insecurity. Limited enforcement capacity leaves strategic resources vulnerable to outside exploitation and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and rail constraints
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity, rail, and port weaknesses limit South Africa's ability to process and export minerals on sovereign terms. Private operators and foreign capital are increasingly important to restoring logistics capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external alignments
frictionVectors.details: Closer BRICS coordination and ties with China and Russia create friction with the United States and European partners. This complicates access to investment, technology, and critical-minerals markets.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to Sudan war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on export routes through war-affected Sudan, leaving oil revenues vulnerable to pipeline damage, blockades, and bargaining by Sudanese armed actors. China remains central to the oil sector while production and fiscal autonomy remain constrained.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and foreign contracting networks
frictionVectors.details: Opaque oil, security, and infrastructure arrangements allow political elites and external firms to capture substantial value. Weak institutions limit public oversight of licensing, revenue transfers, and resource-backed deals.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and ports
External patrons compete over strategic corridors

frictionVectors.title: Gold war economy
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and commercial networks control major gold-producing areas and smuggling routes, while foreign buyers and intermediaries capture value outside formal state channels. Gold revenues help sustain the conflict and weaken national resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and agricultural access
frictionVectors.details: The conflict has made Port Sudan and major transport corridors objects of intense domestic and foreign competition. Gulf, Egyptian, Russian, and other external interests seek influence over ports, farmland, logistics, and security partnerships.

highlights: Resource nationalism paired with selective openness
LNG and corridor projects remain strategic tests

frictionVectors.title: Delayed LNG sovereignty bargain
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large offshore gas development continue to balance national participation and fiscal control against the capital and technology offered by international energy companies. Delays preserve policy space but postpone major export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail competition
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades to Dar es Salaam and strategic rail corridors attract Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and Western financing. Tanzania is seeking diversification, but debt, concession terms, and control of logistics assets remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

highlights: Lomé expands as a regional trade gateway
Phosphate and coastal logistics face external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Port dependency and foreign finance
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a transshipment and regional commerce hub depends heavily on foreign shipping, construction, and finance networks. This strengthens state revenues but leaves strategic infrastructure exposed to external commercial pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate value-chain limits
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources but captures limited value beyond extraction and basic processing. Production, investment, and marketing arrangements remain vulnerable to opaque contracting and foreign price influence.

highlights: Phosphate and energy sectors remain fragile

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCING LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Tunis faces persistent fiscal and balance-of-payments pressure, increasing reliance on bilateral lenders and European financial support. Financing conditions constrain economic policymaking and public investment.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND PHOSPHATE BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic energy output and recurrent phosphate disruptions deepen import dependence and reduce export earnings. Infrastructure and labor disputes continue to limit sovereign control over strategic commodities.

highlights: Oil development advances under foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: EACOP DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Uganda retains formal ownership of its oil resources but depends heavily on foreign firms, lenders, and regional infrastructure to commercialize them. Delays, financing scrutiny, and environmental opposition continue to raise costs and political risks.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL CORRIDOR VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's fuel and export logistics remain exposed to disruptions along the Kenya and Tanzania corridors. This limits Kampala's bargaining power over transport costs and access to external markets.

highlights: Copper strategy is regaining state leverage

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using copper and cobalt demand to seek better investment terms and greater domestic processing, while Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked actors compete for access. Limited refining and power capacity still constrain value capture.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved macroeconomic space but leaves major infrastructure and mining projects dependent on external finance. Electricity shortages remain a direct constraint on mineral sovereignty and industrial expansion.

highlights: Mineral wealth outpaces domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: MINING OWNERSHIP AND OFFTAKE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked firms dominate significant lithium, platinum, gold, and diamond operations, while opaque offtake arrangements can limit fiscal returns. Harare is pressing for local processing but lacks sufficient capital, power, and technology.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND CURRENCY LEAKAGE
frictionVectors.details: Informal gold trading and foreign-currency shortages weaken state revenue collection and monetary control. Sanctions exposure and reliance on non-Western partners further complicate access to finance and infrastructure.
